oracle.concatenation: `${baseUrl}/messages` -- a template literal, so a trailing slash in reverse_proxy survives as a double slash

routing.method: POST only; the pinned router has no other verb on this path
routing.body: express.json(): a malformed body never reaches the handler, and the scenario records what the server answers instead

conventions.markers: request bodies and recorded URLs carry <wire>, <wire-host> and <closed> instead of the run's loopback origins, because a port is host-derived (rule 18); the probe substitutes the live origin before sending and the Go replay substitutes its own peer
conventions.recording: outboundRecording "stub" records the header object the ROUTE passed (the convention other provider fixtures use); "wire" records the headers a real listener received; "none" is the unhooked closed-port boot, where no stub exists to record an attempt
conventions.mocks: each rule is bounded with times:1 so it cannot answer a later request (rule 20)

nodeFetchWireDefaults.measuredBy: the wire.success scenario on an UNHOOKED pinned boot, with the route-managed headers (host, content-length, content-type, anthropic-version, x-api-key) removed; this is what a real peer received, not a claim copied from another route's fixture
nodeFetchWireDefaults.host: the authority differs per run and per peer, so it is asserted separately as Host

success.note: the only scenario that reads a caption; pins the outbound URL, header set, body member order and the 200 body

shapeReason.response.headers.* other than content-ty: express security middleware supplies them; the four named ones are compared because they describe the body
shapeReason.outbound[].headers.connection: the TRANSPORT appends it, not the route: the pinned stub records the header object the route passed and a peer records the framing the client chose, so the value is not a route observable. Presence is still asserted, because a request without a Connection header is a different request
shapeReason.outbound[].headers.content-length: derived from the body, which IS compared byte for byte, and whether a given recording peer exposes it is a property of that peer rather than of the request
shapeReason.outbound[].headers.host: the authority differs per run and per peer; it is asserted as the fact that the request ARRIVED at the peer, plus the recorded path, rather than compared as a value

shapeReason.outboundCount: a rejected fetch never reaches a peer, so the count a peer can observe is 0 on both legs and the pinned count is what the STUB logged before rejecting; the scenario claims the response branch, not the attempt
shapeReason.outbound: the attempt is recorded from the stub, which the Go replay does not have (it reaches the catch through a real closed port)
shapeReason.outbound[].url: recorded from the stub's pre-throw log; no peer receives it on either leg
shapeReason.outbound[].method: recorded from the stub's pre-throw log
shapeReason.outbound[].body: recorded from the stub's pre-throw log
shapeReason.outbound[].headers: recorded from the stub's pre-throw log

body.malformedJson.note: malformed JSON never reaches the handler, so this pins what the server (not the route) answers, with ZERO outbound requests

shapeReason.bodyText: finalhandler renders a development error page whose body embeds the checkout path and a stack trace, so the bytes are host-derived; the VALUE is nulled and the scenario claims only the status and the zero outbound count
shapeReason.contentType: chosen by the same error renderer rather than by the route, so it is not a behaviour this project claims to reproduce
shapeReason.contentLength: derived from the nulled body bytes
shapeReason.etag: derived from the nulled body bytes
shapeReason.outbound: recorded as an EMPTY array because the handler never runs; the count is the compared observable and it is 0
shapeReason.response.headers.*: the error renderer supplies them, not the route
